readerTitle: Why the busiest spot in town can be the wrong one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (케이크 가게, 역사 내 커피 스탠드, 회사 내 IT 헬프데스크) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 입지는 지나가는 사람의 수가 아니라, 내 고객이 살 마음으로 지나가는지와 그 손님 한 명을 얻는 데 드는 임대료로 고른다.
misconception: 유동인구가 많은 곳이 무조건 좋은 입지다. 비싼 임대료는 손님이 많으니 알아서 회수된다.

sources.text: 소매·서비스업 입지 선정의 일반 원칙 (목적형 구매와 편의형 구매의 구분, 임대료를 마케팅 비용으로 보는 관점)

factChecks.note: '목적형 vs 편의형' 구분은 특정 연구가 아니라 소매 입지론의 일반적 설명으로 썼습니다. 특정 연구나 통계를 인용하지 않았는지 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: The busiest spot in town nearly sank this bakery.
body: A bakery known for celebration cakes moved from a quiet side street to a train station concourse. Eight times as many people walked past each day.
Six months later, sales were down and rent had tripled. The cakes were just as good. The spot was the problem.

image.label: A cake shop window in a rushing station crowd
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 역 통로의 작은 케이크 가게 진열창 앞을 수많은 사람이 모션 라인을 그리며 빠르게 지나가고, 아무도 가게를 보지 않음. 실제 역명·브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should the cake shop go?
body: You make custom celebration cakes. Most customers order days ahead and pick up by car.
Three spaces are available. Which do you choose?

options.text: Station concourse: 8,000 people pass daily, rent $9,000 a month
options.feedback: You buy huge visibility, but commuters are rushing and can't carry a large cake onto a train. You pay for traffic that rarely turns into orders.

options.text: Side street near homes, with parking: 1,000 people pass, rent $3,000
options.feedback: Fewer people, but they're locals who can plan, park and pick up. You give up walk-in impulse sales and gain cheap, well-matched customers.

options.text: Mall food court: 4,000 shoppers pass, rent $6,000
options.feedback: Shoppers are in buying mode, which helps. But they want a slice now, not a cake next Saturday, and the parking is a long walk away.

cards.title: Count customers, not people.
body: At the station, 0.25% of passers bought: 20 orders a day. On the side street, many passers were locals coming on purpose, so 3% bought: 30 a day. Over a 30-day month, rent per order was **$15 versus about $3.33**.

cards.title: Choosing a location
body: A good location puts you where **your** customers already are, at the moment they're ready to buy, at a rent that traffic can pay for.

Some purchases are *convenience* buys: coffee, snacks, a phone charger. They live on passing traffic. Others are *destination* buys: cakes, dentists, furniture. People seek them out, so access, parking and nearby customers matter more than crowds.

image.label: Two paths: passing crowd vs customers arriving on purpose
image.brief: 좌우 분할 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Convenience": 많은 사람이 지나가다 일부가 가게로 들어옴. 오른쪽 "Destination": 적은 사람이 차를 몰고 지도 핀을 따라 곧장 가게로 옴.

cards.softwareNote: Online, location is where your product shows up. A top spot in a general app store brings browsers. A listing inside the tool your customers already use, like an integration directory, often brings fewer visitors but more buyers.

cards.title: Four questions before you sign.
body: Ask these about any space, at the hours you'd actually sell:
list: **Who passes?** Are they the customers you need?
**What mode are they in?** Rushing, browsing or ready to buy?
**How do they arrive?** On foot, by car, by train?
**What does each customer cost?** Rent divided by the orders you expect
cards.callout: Rent is partly a marketing cost. Pay it only for traffic you can turn into sales.

cards.title: The same spot can be perfect for someone else.
body: After the bakery left, a coffee stand took over the station space. It thrived.
Commuters wanted something quick, cheap and easy to carry, every morning. The crowd that ignored cakes was exactly right for coffee.
A location isn't good or bad on its own. It fits a business, or it doesn't.

cards.title: Locations are hard to undo.
body: Leases often run for years, and fitting out a space is costly. A mistake here can last longer than most other decisions.

Traffic counts from landlords may come from the wrong hours or count people who never stop. Count yourself, at your selling hours. Check where current customers live, or test with a short pop-up first. Areas also change, so ask what's being built nearby.

cards.title: Now it's a help desk inside a company.
body: You're opening a walk-in IT help desk at headquarters. Field sales staff cause most laptop issues and are only in the building on Monday mornings, on the third floor.
Where do you put the desk?

options.text: The ground-floor lobby, where everyone passes
options.feedback: Very visible, but most people pass on the way to meetings. You'll get quick questions and lines, while field staff still have to come down to find you.

options.text: The third floor, staffed heavily on Monday mornings
options.feedback: You meet your heaviest users where they are, when they're there. You give up general visibility for less wasted time on both sides.

options.text: A cheap back room, with a ticket system instead
options.feedback: It saves space, but a walk-in desk nobody passes isn't really walk-in. Field staff leave on Monday with laptops still broken.

cards.title: Choose the spot where your customers are ready to buy.
body: Crowds are not customers. Match the location to how your customers arrive and what mode they're in, then check the rent against the orders it can bring.
**Try it today:** divide your monthly rent by your monthly number of customers. Ask how many of them came because of where you are.
